s: It is almost midnight, the lights in my bedroom are off and my hands are sweating.
On the screen, a huge figure with a red glow is moving slowly along a corridor, and I am hiding inside a wardrobe, hardly daring to breathe.
I am playing BEAR (Alpha), the Roblox horror game created by Cheedaman in 2019, and I am absolutely terrified.
So why, as soon as the match is over, do I immediately press the button to play again?
According to psychologists, the answer lies in the way our bodies react to danger.
When we are frightened, the brain sends a signal that prepares us either to fight or to run away.
The heart beats faster, we breathe more quickly and the body releases adrenaline, a chemical that makes us feel more alert and full of energy.
In real life, this reaction can save our lives.
In a game, however, it simply gives us a powerful rush of excitement.
The key difference is that, deep down, we know we are safe.
Experts sometimes describe horror games as a kind of rollercoaster for the mind: the fear is real, but the danger is not.
Once the threat has disappeared, the body produces chemicals that make us feel calm and even happy.
Many players say that the moment of relief after a close escape is the best part of the whole experience, and that it is worth every second of panic that came before it.
BEAR (Alpha) is particularly good at creating this feeling.
Survivors cannot see much in the dark, but the Bear always has a red light around it, so you often notice it a moment before it notices you.
Rather than making the game easier, this actually makes it more stressful, because you have to decide in a split second whether to run, hide or stay completely still.
The sound of heavy footsteps getting closer can be far scarier than anything you actually see.
Interestingly, fear is also something we enjoy sharing.
Researchers who study scary entertainment have found that people often feel closer to their friends after going through a frightening experience together.
That certainly matches my own experience.
When my friends and I play online, we scream, laugh at each other and warn each other when the Bear is coming.
By the end of a match, even the players who were caught are usually laughing.
Of course, horror is not for everyone.
Some people find that scary games keep them awake at night or make them anxious, and that is perfectly normal.
Psychologists suggest that the best amount of fear is the amount you can still control.
If a game stops being fun and starts to feel genuinely upsetting, it is a good idea to take a break, play with the lights on or simply choose something different.
As for me, I have learnt a few lessons from all those nights in the wardrobe.
Being scared, it seems, can actually be good for us, as long as we know where the exit is.
So next time you hear those footsteps in the dark, try to remember that your racing heart is just your body doing its job.
And whatever you do, never hide in the same place twice.

s: Ask most people how many basic tastes there are, and they will probably name four: sweet, salty, sour and bitter.
For a long time, scientists in Europe would have given the same answer.
Yet there is a fifth taste that you experience almost every day, whether you are eating a slice of pizza, a bowl of soup or a plate of chips with ketchup.
It is called umami, and the story of how it was discovered begins in a kitchen in Japan more than a century ago.
In 1907, a chemist called Kikunae Ikeda was having dinner at home in Tokyo when he noticed something about the soup his wife had made.
It was dashi, a traditional Japanese stock prepared with a type of seaweed called kombu.
The soup had a rich, savoury flavour that did not seem to fit into any of the four known categories.
Ikeda was so intrigued that he decided to investigate it in his laboratory.
After months of experiments, he managed to isolate the substance responsible for the flavour.
It was glutamate, a natural compound found in many foods.
Ikeda named the taste umami, from a Japanese word that means something like delicious, and in 1908 he published his findings.
Being a practical man, he also developed a way to produce glutamate in the form of a white powder that could be added to food.
It went on sale the following year and became extremely popular in Asian cooking.
Outside Japan, however, many scientists remained unconvinced.
For most of the twentieth century, umami was often dismissed as simply a combination of the other tastes.
It was not until the early two thousands that researchers identified specific receptors on the tongue that react to glutamate.
This discovery finally proved that umami is a separate basic taste, and Ikeda, who had died decades earlier, was shown to have been right all along.
Once you know what umami is, you start to notice it everywhere.
Ripe tomatoes, mushrooms, cheese such as parmesan, cured ham and soy sauce are all rich in glutamate.
In fact, many classic dishes from around the world combine several of these ingredients, which may explain why they are so satisfying.
Some researchers have even suggested that we are born with a liking for umami, since human breast milk contains a high level of glutamate.
Chefs have also learnt to use umami to their advantage.
A little of it can make food taste fuller and more balanced, which means that less salt is needed.
For this reason, some nutritionists believe umami could help people reduce the amount of salt in their diet, especially older people who may have lost some of their sense of taste.
So the next time you take a bite of a cheese and tomato sandwich and think it tastes good, you will know why.
Thanks to one curious scientist and a bowl of soup, we now understand that our tongues are a little more complex than we once believed.

s: On a hot afternoon in July 2021, a thirteen-year-old girl from Japan called Momiji Nishiya stepped onto the podium in Tokyo to receive an Olympic gold medal.
Beside her stood the silver medallist, Rayssa Leal from Brazil, who was also thirteen.
It was the first time skateboarding had ever been included in the Olympic Games, and the youngest athletes in the competition had just made history.
For many people watching around the world, it was a sign of how much the sport had changed.
Skateboarding was born in California in the nineteen fifties, when surfers began attaching wheels to wooden boards so that they could practise their moves on land when the waves were too small.
For several decades, it was seen as a hobby for rebellious teenagers rather than a serious sport.
Skaters were often chased out of car parks and shopping centres, and in some cities skateboarding in public places was even banned.
Yet the culture kept growing.
Skaters invented new tricks, built their own ramps and filmed each other, creating a style that was as much about creativity and self-expression as about competition.
Unlike many traditional sports, there were no coaches, no official rules and no fixed way of doing things.
What mattered was originality, and the respect of other skaters.
When the International Olympic Committee announced in 2016 that skateboarding would be part of the Tokyo Games, the reaction was mixed.
Some skaters were delighted, seeing it as recognition of decades of hard work and a chance to inspire a new generation.
Others were deeply suspicious.
They feared that the Olympics would turn skateboarding into just another sport, with judges, uniforms and strict training programmes, and that its free spirit would be lost.
In the end, many of those fears proved to be exaggerated.
The competitions in Tokyo were relaxed and friendly, and the athletes often celebrated the best tricks of their rivals.
Spectators were particularly struck by the support the skaters gave each other.
After one competitor fell on her final attempt, the others lifted her onto their shoulders.
For some commentators, this spirit was a refreshing contrast to the intense rivalry seen in many other sports.
The Games also had a practical impact.
In several countries, the number of young people taking up skateboarding rose sharply after the Olympics, and many cities began to build new skateparks.
Girls in particular seemed to be inspired by seeing athletes of their own age on the podium.
Sky Brown, who won a bronze medal for Great Britain at the age of thirteen, became a role model for thousands of children.
Of course, the debate has not completely disappeared.
Some skaters still believe that the true heart of skateboarding is on the street, not in a stadium.
But perhaps the two can exist side by side.
After all, every Olympic champion started in the same way: with a board, a bit of concrete and the courage to fall and try again.

s: Palaeontologists are scientists who study life from the distant past.

s: Sixty-six million years ago, an asteroid about ten kilometres wide crashed into what is now Mexico.
The impact caused fires, tsunamis and years of darkness, and around three quarters of all species on Earth disappeared.
Among them, as every schoolchild knows, were the dinosaurs.
Or were they?
According to most palaeontologists today, one group of dinosaurs survived the disaster, and its descendants are still all around us.
You may even have eaten one for lunch.
The idea that birds are living dinosaurs is not as new as it sounds.
In 1861, just two years after Charles Darwin published his theory of evolution, workers in a quarry in Germany found the fossil of a strange creature.
It had teeth, claws on its wings and a long bony tail like a reptile, but it also had clear feathers.
They called it Archaeopteryx, and it immediately became famous as a possible link between reptiles and birds.
For more than a century, however, the connection remained controversial.
Many experts believed that birds had developed from some other group of reptiles, and dinosaurs were generally imagined as slow, cold-blooded giants that had little in common with a sparrow.
That image began to change in the nineteen sixties and seventies, when researchers studying a small, fast predator called Deinonychus noticed how similar its skeleton was to that of a bird.
The most convincing evidence, though, came from China.
In 1996, farmers in the province of Liaoning discovered a small dinosaur whose body was covered in a fine layer of fuzzy filaments, an early form of feathers.
Over the following years, the same region produced dozens of other feathered dinosaurs, preserved in extraordinary detail by volcanic ash.
One of them, Yutyrannus, was a relative of Tyrannosaurus rex, which suggests that even some large meat eaters may have been at least partly covered in feathers.
These discoveries have transformed the way dinosaurs are pictured.
The famous Velociraptor, shown in films as a scaly monster the size of a man, was in reality about as big as a turkey and almost certainly had feathers.
Scientists have also found that many dinosaurs laid eggs in nests, sat on them to keep them warm and had lungs and bones similar to those of modern birds.
Why did feathers appear in the first place?
Interestingly, it seems they did not evolve for flying.
The earliest feathers were probably used to keep warm or to attract a partner, in the same way that a peacock shows off its tail.
Only later did some small dinosaurs begin to use them to glide and eventually to fly.
So when you next see a pigeon in the park or a chicken on a farm, it is worth remembering their family history.
The dinosaurs did not completely vanish when the asteroid hit.
Some of them simply became smaller, grew wings and took to the skies.

s: For more than a thousand years, nobody in the world could read Egyptian hieroglyphs.
Travellers who visited the pyramids and temples saw walls covered in beautiful pictures of birds, eyes, snakes and feet, but they had no idea what they meant.
Many scholars believed that each symbol represented an idea rather than a sound, and that the writing contained secret religious wisdom.

In 1799, French soldiers who had arrived in Egypt with Napoleon were rebuilding an old fort near the town of Rashid, known in Europe as Rosetta, when they found a large slab covered in writing.
They quickly realised it was important.
The stone contained the same text written three times: in hieroglyphs, in a later Egyptian script called Demotic, and in ancient Greek.
Since scholars could still read Greek, the stone offered a unique opportunity to compare the three versions.
However, the stone did not stay in French hands for long.
After the British defeated the French army in Egypt, it was taken to London, where it has been displayed in the British Museum since 1802.
Copies of the inscriptions were sent to experts all over Europe, and a race began to be the first to decipher them.
One of the leading competitors was Thomas Young, a brilliant English scientist who had already made important discoveries about light.
Young made real progress.
He showed that some of the hieroglyphs inside oval shapes, known as cartouches, spelled out the names of kings and queens, and he correctly identified several signs.
But he remained convinced that most hieroglyphs were symbols for ideas, and he could not go further.
The breakthrough came from a young Frenchman, Jean-François Champollion.
He had been fascinated by Egypt since childhood and had learnt an impressive number of languages, including Coptic, a late form of Egyptian still used in church services.
This knowledge proved essential.
By comparing the names in the cartouches with other inscriptions, Champollion realised that hieroglyphs were a mixture of signs that represented sounds and signs that represented ideas.
According to a famous story, when he finally understood the system in 1822, he ran to his brother shouting that he had done it, and then fainted from excitement.
His discovery opened the door to an entire civilisation.
For the first time in centuries, people could read the words of the ancient Egyptians themselves: their prayers, their poems, their letters and even their complaints.
History was no longer only what Greek and Roman writers had said about Egypt.
Today, the Rosetta Stone is one of the most visited objects in the British Museum, and its name has become a symbol of anything that helps to unlock a difficult problem.
Egypt has asked for it to be returned on several occasions, and the debate about where it belongs continues.

s: On a clear night, far from the lights of a city, you can see thousands of stars with the naked eye.
Each of them is a sun, and we now know that many of them have planets travelling around them.
Faced with such enormous numbers, it is hard not to ask one of the oldest questions of all: are we alone in the universe?
For centuries, this was a question for philosophers and science fiction writers.
Today, it is one that scientists are seriously trying to answer.
The search begins surprisingly close to home.
For a long time, Mars was considered the most promising place to look, and several robotic rovers have explored its surface.
They have found clear evidence that rivers and lakes once existed there, billions of years ago, when the planet was warmer and wetter.
If life ever appeared on Mars, scientists hope to find traces of it in ancient rocks, and samples are already being collected for that purpose.
More recently, however, attention has shifted to some unexpected places: the icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn.
Europa, one of the moons of Jupiter, is covered by a thick shell of ice, but beneath it there is thought to be a huge ocean of liquid water.
Enceladus, a small moon of Saturn, is even more intriguing.
In 2005, the Cassini spacecraft observed giant jets of water shooting out of cracks near its south pole.
On Earth, wherever there is liquid water, there is life, so these moons have become top targets for future missions.
Beyond our solar system, the possibilities multiply.
Since the first planets orbiting other stars were confirmed in the nineteen nineties, astronomers have discovered more than five thousand of them.
Some are giant balls of gas, but others are rocky worlds of a similar size to Earth, orbiting at a distance from their star where water could exist as a liquid.
New telescopes are now able to study the atmospheres of a few of these planets, looking for gases that might be produced by living things.
Of course, finding bacteria on a distant moon would be very different from meeting intelligent beings.
Since 1960, some researchers have been listening for radio signals from other civilisations, so far without success.
This silence has led to a famous puzzle, known as the Fermi paradox.
If the universe is so vast and so old, and life is not unusual, then where is everybody?
There are many possible answers.
Perhaps intelligent life is extremely rare.
Perhaps civilisations exist but are too far away, or communicate in ways we do not understand.
Some scientists even suggest that we simply have not been searching for long enough, since our technology has existed for only a tiny fraction of the history of the universe.
Whatever the truth, the search itself is changing the way we see our own planet.
Every discovery reminds us how special the conditions on Earth are.

s: One night in 2016, staff at the National Aquarium of New Zealand discovered that one of their residents had disappeared.

Despite their intelligence, octopuses live surprisingly short lives.

Some scientists believe this is one reason why their behaviour is so fascinating: unlike humans, they cannot learn from their parents, so almost everything they know must be discovered by themselves.
As for Inky, nobody knows what happened to him after his great escape.

s: In 1941, a Swiss engineer called George de Mestral returned from a walk in the mountains with his dog and noticed that both his trousers and the fur of the dog were covered in burrs, the small seed heads of a common plant.

s: When most people think of Minecraft, they imagine someone building a house, digging for diamonds or running away from a creeper.
With more than three hundred million copies sold, it is the best-selling video game of all time, and for millions of players that is exactly what it is: a fun way to spend an afternoon.

Perhaps the most surprising use of Minecraft, however, has nothing to do with science.
In 2020, the organisation Reporters Without Borders opened the Uncensored Library, an enormous digital building inside the game.
Its shelves contain articles by journalists whose work has been banned in their own countries.
The idea was clever: in places where news websites are blocked, Minecraft is often still available, so young people can find the articles by visiting the library in the game.
Not everyone is convinced, of course.

Others point out that a game cannot replace a good teacher, however popular it is.
Even so, it is difficult to deny that Minecraft has become something unusual: a tool as much as a toy.
The blocks are the same for everyone, but what people build with them depends entirely on their imagination.
And if a group of players can build a computer, a classroom and a library out of nothing but virtual cubes, it is hard to say where the limits really are.

s: In a library at Yale University in the United States, there is a small book that has defeated some of the most brilliant minds of the last hundred years.
It contains around two hundred and forty pages of elegant handwriting, accompanied by colourful drawings of plants, stars and strange human figures.
The problem is that nobody knows what language it is written in, or whether it is a language at all.
The book is known as the Voynich manuscript, after Wilfrid Voynich, a Polish bookseller who bought it in 1912 from a religious college near Rome.
Voynich was convinced that he had found something extraordinary and spent the rest of his life trying to understand it, without success.
Since then, the manuscript has been studied by professional codebreakers, linguists, historians and thousands of enthusiastic amateurs.
All of them have failed.
We do know a few things about it.
In 2009, scientists used radiocarbon dating to analyse the animal skin on which the book is written, and concluded that it was made in the early fifteenth century, between about 1404 and 1438.
This ruled out one popular theory, which claimed that the book was a fake created by Voynich himself.
Letters found with the manuscript also show that it once belonged to an emperor in Prague, who is said to have paid a large amount of gold for it.
The contents, however, remain a complete mystery.
About half of the book is filled with drawings of plants, but most of them do not match any species known to science.
Other sections seem to show astronomical charts, while one particularly odd part contains images of small figures bathing in pools connected by pipes.
The text itself uses an alphabet of around twenty to thirty symbols that appear nowhere else.
Over the years, people have suggested all kinds of explanations.
Some believe it is written in a secret code designed to hide medical or scientific knowledge.
Others think it may be an unknown language written in an invented alphabet.
Statistical studies have shown that the text has some patterns typical of real languages, which makes it unlikely to be completely random.
Yet every few years, someone announces that they have finally solved the puzzle, and every time their solution is quickly rejected by other experts.
Some researchers suspect that the most disappointing answer may also be the correct one: that the book is an elaborate hoax from the fifteenth century, written to impress or deceive a wealthy buyer.
If so, its author would have needed great patience, since producing so many pages of convincing nonsense would have been extremely difficult.
Whatever its origin, the manuscript has become famous precisely because it refuses to give up its secret.
Today, anyone can look at every page online, and new theories appear constantly.
Perhaps one day someone will finally read it.
Until then, it remains one of the most fascinating puzzles in the world.

s: In January 1995, a small group of grey wolves was released into Yellowstone National Park in the United States.
For most visitors, it was simply a chance to see a magnificent animal in the wild.
For scientists, however, it was the beginning of one of the most closely watched experiments in the history of ecology.
Wolves had been absent from the park for around seventy years, and nobody knew exactly what would happen when they returned.
The wolves had not disappeared by accident.

In the early twentieth century, they were seen as dangerous pests that killed farm animals, and they were hunted, trapped and poisoned until the last ones in the park were gone by the nineteen twenties.
At the time, this was considered a success.
Without their main predator, however, the number of elk, a large kind of deer, grew rapidly.
The elk ate young trees and bushes, especially along the rivers, and some areas of the park began to look bare.
When the wolves came back, the most obvious change was that the number of elk fell.
But many researchers believe that something more subtle also happened.
The elk seemed to change their behaviour, spending less time in open valleys and along riverbanks, where they could easily be ambushed.
In some of those places, young willows and aspens, which had struggled to grow for decades, began to recover.
According to this view, the effects did not stop there.
As trees returned along the rivers, beavers came back too, using the wood to build dams that created ponds and wetlands for fish, frogs and birds.
The carcasses left by wolves provided food for ravens, eagles and even bears.

Scientists call this kind of chain reaction a trophic cascade, and the story of Yellowstone became one of the most famous examples in the world, especially after a short online video about it was watched by millions of people.
More recently, however, some ecologists have argued that the popular version of the story is too simple.
They point out that other factors were also changing at the same time.
Hunting by humans outside the park reduced the number of elk, the population of bears increased, and a series of dry years affected the plants.
In some areas, the trees have recovered far less than the famous video suggests.
The wolves, these researchers say, played a part, but they were not the only reason for the changes.
This debate does not mean that the return of the wolves was unimportant.
On the contrary, it shows how complex natural systems are, and how difficult it can be to separate cause and effect.
Most scientists agree that predators play a vital role in keeping ecosystems healthy, even if their influence varies from place to place.
Today, around one hundred wolves live in the park, and they are one of its main attractions.
Their story is a reminder that every species is connected to many others, and that removing just one of them can have consequences that take decades to understand.

s: If you were asked to name the most dangerous animal in the world, you would probably think of a shark, a lion or perhaps a crocodile.
These predators certainly have sharp teeth and a frightening reputation, but together they kill only a few hundred people a year.
The real champion is far smaller, weighs less than a grain of rice and may well be flying around your bedroom tonight: the mosquito.
Mosquitoes are not dangerous because of their bite, which is usually nothing more than an itchy red spot.
The problem is what they can carry.
When a mosquito feeds on the blood of an infected person or animal, tiny parasites or viruses can travel into its body.
The next time it bites someone, it may pass them on.
In this way, mosquitoes spread diseases such as malaria, dengue and yellow fever, which together cause hundreds of thousands of deaths every year, mainly in tropical countries.
Surprisingly, only female mosquitoes bite.
Males live on the sugar found in flowers and fruit, and so do females most of the time.
However, a female needs the protein in blood in order to produce her eggs.
To find a victim, she relies on an impressive set of senses.
She can detect the carbon dioxide we breathe out from several metres away, and as she gets closer, she follows the heat and the smell of our skin.
That is why some people seem to be bitten far more often than others.
Their bite is also more sophisticated than it looks.
A mosquito does not simply stab the skin with a single needle.
Its mouth contains six thin parts that work together: some cut through the skin, one searches for a blood vessel and another injects saliva.
The saliva stops the blood from clotting and, conveniently for the insect, it also makes the bite almost painless at first.
By the time we notice the itch, the mosquito has usually flown away.
Fighting such a tiny enemy has never been easy.
For decades, people have relied on insecticides, mosquito nets and draining the still water where mosquitoes lay their eggs.
Nets treated with insecticide have saved millions of lives, especially among young children.
However, many mosquitoes have become resistant to the chemicals, so scientists are looking for new solutions.
Some of these solutions sound like science fiction.
In several countries, researchers have released mosquitoes carrying a natural type of bacteria called Wolbachia, which makes it much harder for the insects to pass on certain viruses.
Others are developing genetically modified mosquitoes that produce offspring unable to survive.
In addition, the first vaccines against malaria have recently been approved, which many experts see as a historic step.
Not everyone agrees that we should try to get rid of mosquitoes completely, however.
They are food for birds, bats, fish and frogs, and some ecologists warn that removing them could have consequences we cannot predict.
For now, the battle continues, and it is a reminder that in nature, size is not everything.
The most dangerous creature on the planet is not the one with the biggest teeth, but the one we can barely see.

s: In 1951, a British businessman called Sir Hugh Beaver was out hunting in Ireland when he got into an argument with his friends.
They wanted to know which was the fastest game bird in Europe, but none of the reference books in the house could give them an answer.
Beaver, who was the managing director of the Guinness brewery, realised that people in pubs all over the country must be having similar arguments every night.
What they needed, he thought, was a book that could settle them.
To write it, he hired two twin brothers, Norris and Ross McWhirter, who ran a fact-finding agency in London and were known for their extraordinary memory for facts and figures.
The first edition of the Guinness Book of Records was published in 1955.
To the surprise of almost everyone, it became a bestseller by Christmas.
Since then, the book has been translated into dozens of languages, and it is now one of the best-selling books in the world.
But a book of records is only useful if people can trust it.
Today, that responsibility belongs to a team of official adjudicators, the judges who decide whether a record has really been broken.

Their job takes them all over the world, from schools and shopping centres to television studios, and they may spend one day counting hula hoops and the next measuring the longest fingernails on the planet.
Breaking a record is not as simple as doing something impressive.
First, the challenger must apply and receive a set of guidelines, which explain exactly how the attempt must be carried out.
These rules can be surprisingly strict.
For a food record, for example, all of the food usually has to be eaten afterwards rather than wasted.
For a distance record, the measuring equipment may need to be checked by an expert beforehand.
Not every attempt has an adjudicator present.
Many people instead send in evidence, such as videos, photographs and statements from independent witnesses, which is then carefully examined by the team.
This process can take several weeks, and many applications are rejected, often because a small rule was not followed.
Some challengers are disappointed, but the adjudicators insist that the rules are what give a record its value.
Certain records are no longer accepted at all.

Over the years, the organisation has stopped monitoring challenges that could put people or animals in danger, such as eating the most of something in a very short time or making a pet as heavy as possible.
The aim, they say, is to celebrate achievement, not to encourage people to harm themselves.
Interestingly, the question that started it all has never been fully answered.
The fastest game bird in Europe is often said to be the golden plover, but experts still disagree about how such a thing should be measured.
Perhaps that is fitting.
As the adjudicators know better than anyone, a record is only as good as the evidence behind it.

s: A speedrun is a special way to play a video game.

s: Super Mario Bros. came out in 1985.
It is one of the most famous games in history.
Millions of people played it as children.
But for speedrunners, it became a race that never ends.

Speedrunners finish it in less than five minutes.
How did they do it?
They used warp pipes to skip worlds, and they discovered tiny tricks to save time.
For many years, players fought for every hundredth of a second.
In 2018 a runner called Kosmic got a very fast time.

Did they play for fun?

s: Video games are made by people, and people make mistakes.
A glitch is an error in the code of a game.
For most players, glitches are annoying.
For speedrunners, they are treasure.
Some glitches allow you to walk through walls.
Others let you skip whole levels or even jump straight to the final scene.
Finding these errors involves testing the game in strange ways, like pausing at a precise moment or walking against a corner for minutes.
Speedrunners love sharing their discoveries.
When someone finds a new glitch, the community starts practicing it immediately.
Many tricks require pressing buttons in a window of a few milliseconds, so executing them is incredibly hard.
Because glitches can change a game completely, speedrunners divide their races into categories.
In an any% run, using glitches is allowed.
In a glitchless run, players avoid using any error.
This way, everyone competes under the same rules.
Some developers hate their games being broken, but many enjoy watching speedruns.
A few even include secret shortcuts on purpose.
After all, finding new ways to play is part of the fun of gaming.

s: It is three in the morning, and more than one hundred thousand people are watching a young woman try to finish a video game from the nineties in under an hour.
Behind her, a small crowd is cheering, and in a corner of the screen a number keeps rising: the amount of money that viewers have donated to charity.
This is Games Done Quick, a week-long marathon of speedruns that takes place twice a year and has become one of the most unusual fundraising events in the world.
The idea started in a surprisingly modest way.
In 2010, a group of speedrunners met in a basement in the United States and streamed their runs online, asking viewers to donate to a charity.
They hoped to raise a few thousand dollars.
Instead, they collected over ten thousand.
Encouraged by this success, they organised another event, and then another.
Today the marathons are held in large hotel conference rooms, the runs are broadcast without a break for seven days, and the total raised over the years has reached tens of millions of dollars.
Each marathon supports a different cause.

The winter event, held in January, raises money for an organisation that fights cancer, while the summer event supports Doctors Without Borders, which provides medical care in war zones and areas hit by disasters.
For many viewers, this is what makes the marathons special.
They are not only watching incredible skill; they are also helping people they will never meet.
The organisers have found creative ways to encourage donations.
Viewers can pay to choose the name of a character, vote on which path a runner should take or unlock an extra challenge, such as completing a level with their eyes closed.
Runners often explain the tricks they are using as they play, so even people who know nothing about the game can follow what is happening.
The atmosphere is friendly and enthusiastic, and mistakes are greeted with sympathy rather than criticism.
Behind the scenes, the event requires an enormous amount of preparation.
Hundreds of runners apply to take part, and a selection committee watches their videos to decide who will appear.
Every run must be entertaining, reliable and safe for a general audience.

Volunteers work in shifts to control the cameras, read out donation messages and keep the schedule on time, which is no easy task when a single unexpected glitch can make a run last twenty minutes longer than planned.
Not every runner finds the experience easy.
Performing a run in front of a live audience is very different from practising alone at home, and even experienced players admit that their hands shake when they sit down.
Yet most of them say the pressure is worth it.
For a community that is often seen as strange or antisocial, the marathons are a chance to show what gamers can do when they work together.
Perhaps that is the real secret of their success.
Speedrunning is usually about individuals racing against the clock.
At Games Done Quick, however, the most important number on the screen is not the time, but the total at the bottom: proof that a hobby can make a real difference.
